extracted.intended_audience: graduate students, literary scholars, and critics studying narratology and narrative temporality
extracted.subtask_description: Analysing and classifying a narrative's temporal organization: order (anachrony/achrony/syllepsis), duration (anisochronies, pacing), and canonical tempo-forms (pause, scene, summary, ellipsis), with methods for segmenting large narrative units and approximating chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anachronies (analepses and prolepses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retrospection and anticipation in narrative are christened analepses (retrospections) and prolepses (anticipations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These operations disturb simple chronological sequence: examples in Proust include proleptic analepses and analeptic prolepses (e.g., indications that 'it will be reported to me a few years later'). Double structures (proleptic analepses and analeptic prolepses) can invert relationships between narrative anachronies and story-order, producing retrospective advance notices or anticipatory recalls (formulas like 'It would happen later, as we have already seen'). Analyze their effects on reader temporality and on the relation between narrative-order and story-order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Achrony
rubrics_metrics.description: Events or anecdotes provided with no temporal reference at all, which cannot be placed earlier or later in relation to surrounding events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such dateless incidents are attached to the commentarial discourse rather than positioned diachronically in the story; treat them as achronies (e.g., an anecdote implying later social progress but with no textual anchor). They indicate the narrative's capacity to disengage arrangement from chronological dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open analepses
rubrics_metrics.description: Analepses whose conclusion cannot be localized in time, producing temporally indefinite narrative sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that open analepses entail indefinite temporal spans within the text and may require treating the section as temporally indefinite for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double anachrony / retrospective advance notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative contortions where an advance notice in the diegetic time refers to an event already covered by the narrative (or vice versa), so that later is earlier and earlier later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These produce a zigzag effect for the reader and must be handled carefully when defining direction of movement; catalog instances and analyze how they reframe events already read or yet to come.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllepsis (grouping by kinship: geographical or thematic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The taking together (syllepsis) of anachronic groupings governed by a kinship (spatial, temporal, or thematic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify geographical syllepsis (voyage narratives that group anecdotes by stops) and thematic syllepsis (classical episodic novels that insert stories by analogy or contrast). Syllepsis explains narrative groupings that defy simple chronological succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative vs story order (narrative autonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative's syntagmatic (textual) order can be independent of, or governed by criteria other than, the story's chronological order (e.g., spatial proximity, climatic identity, thematic kinship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not naively equate narrative sequence with story chronology; examine whether ordering is driven by locations, themes, or oppositions (examples: Meseglise way vs Guermantes way in Proust).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for demarcating large narrative articulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose demarcation of large narrative units by the presence of an important temporal and/or spatial break rather than by external chapter divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use significant temporal/spatial discontinuities to define units (the text gives an operational carving of Recherche into 11 units); note that external divisions (parts, chapters) often do not coincide with internal articulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anisochronies (duration and rhythm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations in narrative 'speed' (relationship between story-time and narrative length) that emancipate narrative from story temporality; anisochronies are as important as anachronies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define speed as ratio duration-of-story/length-of-text. Because exact diegetic time is usually imprecise, analyze anisochronies at a macroscopic/statistical level across large narrative units rather than micro-measuring them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isochronous narrative (theoretical reference zero)
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothetical narrative with unchanging speed where the relation duration-of-story/length-of-text remains steady (isochrony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this as an ideal laboratory construct that ordinarily does not exist in literature; it serves as a reference to detect accelerations and slowdowns in real narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring narrative speed (NT vs ST)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationalize tempo by contrasting NT (narrative time, length of text) with ST (story time, duration in diegetic time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use NT and ST to classify movements; because measurement is imprecise, adopt approximate, large-scale chronologies and accept statistical approximations for lengths and durations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive pause (pause)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative movement where narrative discourse corresponds to a nonexistent diegetic duration (NT = infinite, ST = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish descriptive pause from mere description and from authorial intrusions; descriptive pauses are diegetic and constitute canonical slow movements in narrative tempo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative movement usually realized in dialogue that conventionally approximates equality between narrative time and story time (NT = ST).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat scenes as giving 'a sort of equality' between NT and ST but not as rigorous temporal indicators; scenes report everything said but not the precise speed of utterance or pauses in conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement with variable tempo that covers the range between scene and ellipsis (NT < ST).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary is flexible in pace and historically the form that covered many days/months/years in a few pages in the novel tradition; identify where the text condenses extended story time into shorter narrative space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative movement where narrative time is absent for some story duration (NT = 0, ST = n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ellipses correspond to omissions of story time in the narrative; large ellipses are central to rhythms like Proust's increasing discontinuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of canonical 'slow-motion' (NT > ST) form
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no canonical narrative form symmetrical to summary where NT > ST (a genuine scene in slow motion); such experiments exist but are not established canonical forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that very long 'slow-motion' scenes in practice are usually extended by extranarrative insertions (memories, descriptions), not by a pure NT>ST slowing of events; treat such instances as deliberate, non-canonical experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical selection of four narrative movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative tradition has selected four basic temporal movements as canonical: pause, scene, summary, and ellipsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four categories as an analytical taxonomy analogous to musical movements when describing a novel's tempo structure and alternations; map sections of text to these canonical movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological limitation: macroscopic/statistical analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Because diegetic time is almost never indicated precisely, duration analysis is relevant only at the macroscopic level of large narrative units and must be treated as statistical approximation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate pages/sections into large units and approximate story durations; avoid claims of precision for micro-temporal measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing internal chronology (practical guideline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct an approximately clear and coherent internal chronology using main external reference points while acknowledging contradictions and indeterminacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve contradictory chronological signals (external historical references vs internal sequence) by adhering to main coherent series and treating ambiguous episodes as exceptions; adopt an indicative chronology for rhythm analysis rather than absolute dating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proustian rhythm: increasing discontinuity and slowing down
rubrics_metrics.description: A discernible internal evolution in Proust where narrative slows (enormous scenes covering short story-time) and is compensated by more and larger ellipses, yielding greater discontinuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing Proust (or similar texts), look for this pattern: very long scene-pages devoted to minutes/hours, alternating with ellipses covering years; quantify approximately (the text gives page:time sketches) to demonstrate the trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical ordering as narrative principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic/situational ordering (stations, walks, routes) can determine narrative succession independently of chronological sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify sequences grouped by place (e.g., train stops, walks) where the narrator orders anecdotes by site-proximity or thematic kinship rather than by temporal causality; treat such ordering as another form of narrative autonomy.
